A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
star clusters formed from turbulent clumps are very extended at early times.

star formation from clumps in the observed mass range, with star formation efficiencies in the range 10-30% and with primordial binary fractions, binary eccentricities and mass segregation levels similar to those observed, is not consistent with the formation of young star clusters in the observed mass, size and age ranges.
the formation timescale of the clusters is too short compared to observed timescales.
The main takeaway from our work is that

star clusters are likely not born in their present state, but are instead born as very different systems that expand rapidly, and then are modified through dynamical interactions and mass loss over the next 100 Myr.
the fast star cluster formation scenario, where stars are formed from a single clump and then the gas is instantaneously expelled, cannot explain the observed young cluster properties.
the fast formation limit is not realistic for the formation of young star clusters.
